source_metadata.title: The Impact of a Reported Penicillin Allergy on Surgical Site Infection Risk

atoms.canonical_statement: The study assessed whether a reported penicillin allergy was associated with surgical site infection risk among patients undergoing five major procedure types.
The investigators conducted a retrospective cohort study at Massachusetts General Hospital using procedures performed from 2010 through 2014.
The cohort included hip arthroplasty, knee arthroplasty, hysterectomy, colon surgery, and coronary artery bypass grafting procedures.

population.label: Patients undergoing HPRO, KPRO, HYST, COLO, or CABG

atoms.canonical_statement: Patient data came from the Partners HealthCare Enterprise Data Warehouse, with procedure and SSI data compiled and reported to NHSN by the MGH Infection Control Unit.
Reported penicillin allergy was defined as any historically documented allergy to a penicillin antibiotic at surgery, including hypersensitivity reactions, side effects, and intolerances.

exposures.details: Historically documented penicillin allergy at surgery regardless of stated reaction

atoms.canonical_statement: For patients with multiple procedures, penicillin allergy status from the first procedure was used for exposure classification.

Penicillin reactions were classified from coded and free-text data as hypersensitivity, side effect/intolerance/toxicity, or unknown, with separate identification of potential beta-lactam contraindications and reactions eligible for allergy evaluation.
The primary outcome was NHSN-defined surgical site infection, including superficial, deep, and organ-space SSI.

outcome.definition: NHSN-defined superficial, deep, or organ-space SSI for each procedure
outcome.measurement_method: Prospective infection-control surveillance with 100% chart review

atoms.canonical_statement: Eight experienced infection control practitioners prospectively surveilled SSIs by reviewing 100% of procedures and applying standardized NHSN definitions.
The secondary outcome was perioperative antibiotic use from 120 minutes before surgery through the end of surgery.

outcome.definition: Antibiotics administered from 120 minutes before surgery until the end of surgery

atoms.canonical_statement: The analysis separately evaluated preincision antibiotics started within 120 minutes before incision and vancomycin initiation within the recommended 60 to 120 minutes before incision.

The adjusted SSI analysis used multivariable logistic regression with generalized estimating equations for repeated procedures; the final model included age, sex, race, surgery type, ASA class, procedure duration, and wound class.
A marginal structural model estimated whether receipt of only beta-lactam alternative antibiotics mediated the association between reported penicillin allergy and SSI.

The number needed to evaluate calculation assumed that 90% to 100% of patients with reported penicillin allergy were not truly allergic and that delabeled patients would receive first-line beta-lactam prophylaxis.
The cohort contained 8385 patients and 9004 surgical procedures.
The 9004 procedures comprised 2624 hip arthroplasties, 2439 knee arthroplasties, 1560 hysterectomies, 1250 colon surgeries, and 1131 CABG procedures.
Among 8385 patients, 922 patients, 11.0%, had a reported penicillin allergy.
The 922 patients with reported penicillin allergy had 1042 documented reactions, including 718 hypersensitivity reactions, 89 side effects or toxicities, and 235 reactions of unknown type.
The most common documented hypersensitivity reactions were rash in 346 patients, urticaria in 166, and angioedema or swelling in 82.

Five documented hypersensitivity reactions were considered potential contraindications to beta-lactam administration: two acute interstitial nephritis reactions, two blistering reactions, and one Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis reaction.
Of 1042 documented penicillin reactions, 953, 92.0%, were considered amenable to standard penicillin allergy evaluation with skin testing and/or drug challenge.
Patients with reported penicillin allergy were slightly older and more often female and White than patients without a reported allergy.

Cardiovascular disease was less common and asthma and prior VRE colonization or infection were more common in the reported-allergy group; diabetes, malignancy, chronic renal impairment, and MRSA flags were not materially different.
Procedure mix and wound class differed by allergy status, while procedure duration was similar; trauma procedures were slightly more frequent in the reported-allergy group.
Across 9004 procedures, 241 SSIs occurred, an overall rate of 2.7%.

atoms.canonical_statement: Among 7893 procedures not using both antibiotic classes, beta-lactam antibiotics were initiated in the preoperative window in 98.2% versus 96.0% for beta-lactam alternatives, P<.001.

Among recipients of cefazolin or vancomycin, 97.5% of vancomycin recipients were outside the recommended 60 to 120 minute preincision window, compared with 1.7% of cefazolin recipients outside their recommended timing window, P<.001.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: vancomycin group percentage outside timing window

atoms.canonical_statement: Vancomycin was initiated a median of 24 minutes before incision, with an interquartile range of 13 to 35 minutes.

atoms.canonical_statement: The modeled number needed to evaluate was 112 to 124 patients with reported penicillin allergy to prevent one SSI.

atoms.canonical_statement: No antibiotic was administered within the specified preincision window for 2.9% of procedures with reported penicillin allergy and 2.3% without reported penicillin allergy, P=.23.
The authors concluded that the higher SSI odds associated with a reported penicillin allergy were attributable to use of second-line perioperative antibiotics.
The authors proposed systematic preoperative penicillin allergy evaluation as a way to improve prophylactic antibiotic selection and potentially reduce SSI risk.
The authors stated that all but five patients with reported penicillin allergy should have been able to receive cefazolin directly or undergo outpatient penicillin allergy evaluation before surgery.
The study was retrospective, which limits causal inference despite use of prospectively collected procedure and SSI data and manual validation of key allergy data.
Only 241 SSI events occurred, preventing simultaneous adjustment for every possible confounder.
The small number of SSI events left the study underpowered for surgery-specific subgroup analyses.
The data came from one academic medical center, so patients, providers, prophylaxis practices, and allergy-specialist access may differ elsewhere.
SSI ascertainment methods are not standardized across institutions; the authors argued that any surveillance differences should be unrelated to penicillin-allergy exposure.

The study reported support from NIH K01AI125631, the American Academy of Allergy Asthma and Immunology Foundation, NIH K01AI110524, the MGH-MIT Grand Challenge, and Harvard Catalyst/NIH UL1 TR001102 with affiliated institutional contributions.
All authors reported no conflicts of interest relevant to the manuscript.
